prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I can love both fair and brown, Her whom abundance melts, and her whom want betrays, Her who loves loneness best, and her who masks and plays, Her whom the country formed, and whom the town, Her who believes, and her who tries, Her who still weeps with spongy eyes, And her who is dry cork, and never cries; I can love her, and her, and you, and you, I can love any, so she be not true. Will no other vice content you? Will it not serve your turn to do as did your mothers? Or have you all old vices spent, and now would find out others? Or doth a fear that men are true torment you? O we are not, be not you so; Let me, and do you, twenty know. Rob me, but bind me not, and let me go. Must I, who came to travail thorough you, Grow your fixed subject, because you are true? Venus heard me sigh this song, And by love's sweetest part, variety, she swore, She heard not this till now; and that it should be so no more. She went, examined, and returned ere long, And said, Alas! some two or three Poor heretics in love there be, Which think to ’stablish dangerous constancy. But I have told them, Since you will be true, You shall be true to them who are false to you.

outputs.L1:
I can love both fair and brown:  
Her whom abundance melts, and her whom want betrays;  
Her who loves loneliness best, and her who masks and plays;  
Her whom the country formed, and her whom the town;  
Her who believes, and her who tries;  
Her who still weeps with spongy eyes,  
And her who is dry cork and never cries.  
I can love her, and her, and you, and you;  
I can love any, so she be not true.

Will no other vice content you?  
Will it not serve your turn to do as did your mothers?  
Or have you spent all old vices  
And now would find out others?  
Or doth the fear that men are true torment you?  
Oh, we are not—be not you so.  
Let me, and do you, twenty know;  
Rob me, but bind me not, and let me go.  
Must I, who came to travail through you,  
Become your fixed subject because you are true?

Venus heard me sigh this song,  
And by love’s sweetest part—variety—she swore  
That she had never heard this before,  
And that it should be so no more.  
She went, examined, and returned ere long,  
And said, “Alas! Some two or three  
Poor heretics in love there be  
Who think to establish dangerous constancy.  
But I have told them: since you will be true,  
You shall be true to those who are false to you.”
outputs.L2:
I can desire women pale or dark:  
the one softened by wealth, and the one whose poverty shows;  
the woman who prefers solitude, and the one who disguises herself and performs;  
the one shaped by rural life, and the one raised in the city;  
the believer and the skeptic;  
the woman whose absorbent eyes continually overflow,  
and the woman as dry as cork, who never sheds a tear.  
I can love this woman, that woman, you, and you—  
any woman at all, provided she is not faithful.

Can no other fault satisfy you?  
Is it not enough to behave as your mothers did?  
Have you exhausted every vice of the past  
and decided to invent a new one?  
Or are you troubled by the fear that men might be loyal?  
We are not, so do not be loyal yourselves.  
Let me know twenty women, and you should know twenty men.  
Take what you can from me, but do not tie me down; let me leave.  
Must I, who came only to journey through your love,  
become your permanent subject simply because you are faithful?

Venus heard me lament in this song.  
Swearing by love’s sweetest quality—variety—  
she declared that she had never before heard of such behavior  
and promised it would not continue.  
She left to investigate and soon returned, saying:

“Sadly, there are two or three  
poor heretics in matters of love  
who seek to establish the dangerous doctrine of constancy.  
But I have given them this command:  
since they insist on being faithful,  
they must devote that faith to lovers who will betray them.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker boasts that his capacity for love is virtually limitless: he can be attracted to women of every appearance, temperament, social background, and emotional disposition. Yet there is one quality he cannot tolerate—faithfulness. Rather than seeking a devoted lover, he prefers women who are untrue, because their inconstancy allows him the same freedom to pursue other women without guilt or obligation.

He therefore urges women to embrace familiar, traditional vices instead of introducing what he mockingly calls the disturbing novelty of constancy. To him, betrayal, deception, and mutual exploitation are preferable to the restrictions imposed by sincere devotion. He would rather be deceived or used by a lover than find himself bound by her loyalty.

In the end, Venus issues an appropriately ironic decree. The small number of women who stubbornly insist on remaining faithful will not be rewarded with equally devoted partners. Instead, they will be paired with men who betray them, ensuring that even constancy is met with falsehood.
outputs.L4:
In John Donne’s “The Indifferent,” the speaker presents himself as capable of loving almost any kind of woman. He catalogs women of different appearances, temperaments, social backgrounds, and habits: fair and dark, rich and poor, solitary and sociable, emotional and restrained, rural and urban. His apparent openness, however, depends on one condition—none of these women must be faithful. What initially sounds like a celebration of romantic inclusiveness therefore becomes a comic defense of promiscuity and emotional freedom.

The speaker treats constancy not as a virtue but as an unreasonable burden. He urges women to follow the supposedly unfaithful example of earlier generations and insists that men themselves are not true. In his view, mutual inconstancy allows both partners to pursue multiple lovers without becoming bound to one another. He would rather be deceived than possessed: a woman may “rob” him emotionally, but she must not restrict his liberty by expecting a permanent commitment. Donne thus satirically reverses the conventional language of courtly love, portraying fidelity as a strange vice and betrayal as the more natural arrangement.

In the final stanza, Venus, the goddess of love, hears the speaker’s argument and approvingly associates love with variety. After investigating, she discovers that only a few women still believe in “dangerous constancy.” These faithful women are treated as heretics because they resist the poem’s inverted code of love. Venus punishes them by ensuring that, although they remain true, their lovers will be false to them. The ending completes the poem’s cynical joke: faithfulness brings neither moral reward nor romantic happiness, but suffering and betrayal. Through exaggeration, paradox, and irony, the poem exposes the speaker’s selfish desire for freedom while playfully overturning traditional ideals of loyalty and devoted love.
outputs.L5:
### Her, And, Will

She carried the memory of **Her** past like a letter folded close to the heart. **And** though the road ahead was uncertain, she kept walking. Courage, she learned, was not the absence of fear—it was the **Will** to move forward despite it.

She heard not this till now; and that it should be so no more.  
She went, examined, and returned ere long,  
And said, “Alas! some two or three  
Poor heretics in love there be,  
Which think to stablish dangerous constancy.
